analysis.one_liner: Stops health insurers from cutting provider pay or dropping doctors during declared health emergencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee; no committee acted on it and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During a federally declared public health emergency, this bill would bar private health insurers and employer plans from cutting the rates they pay doctors and hospitals, or from ending contracts with providers, unless the move was based on fraud, abuse, or quality concerns. It would apply retroactively to the COVID-19 emergency declared in January 2020. The idea is that patients shouldn't lose access to their own doctors mid-crisis because an insurer decides to squeeze providers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with private insurance who live where a public health emergency has been declared. The bill keeps their doctors in-network and keeps reimbursement levels from being slashed while the emergency runs, so they can keep getting care from the providers they already use. Doctors and hospitals also benefit because their contract terms are locked in during a crisis.

how_it_helps.text: During a declared public health emergency, insurers and employer health plans could not pay a doctor less than they would have the day before the emergency started, and could not terminate the provider's contract, except for fraud, abuse, quality concerns, or federal exclusion-list reasons.

The rule would apply retroactively to public health emergencies declared on or after January 31, 2020, covering the COVID-19 emergency, and would be written into the public health, employer-benefit (ERISA), and tax laws so it reaches group plans, individual market insurance, and self-insured employer plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, which would lose the ability to cut provider reimbursement rates or drop providers to control costs during an emergency. Some of that cost could be passed back to consumers as higher premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers argue that during a crisis they may genuinely need to adjust rates or network contracts to keep premiums affordable, and the bill removes that tool even though it carves out fraud, abuse, and quality concerns. The cost of freezing rates could show up in premiums paid by the same consumers the bill aims to protect.

The protection is temporary and narrow: it applies only while a federally declared emergency lasts and only in the declared emergency area, so it does nothing about insurer rate cuts or contract terminations in ordinary times, which is when most of them happen.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it protects continuity of care for insured patients during emergencies, a period when losing your doctor is most damaging. The cost is that insurers lose a cost-control lever during exactly the period when claims spike, which could pressure premiums. A fair-minded reading is that the bill targets a genuine gap in consumer protection but is a narrow, emergency-only patch rather than a fix for network and reimbursement problems overall.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and split among three House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on June 18, 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, joined by Rep. Rosa DeLauro.
The House referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — a routing that requires any of them to act before the bill can move.
No committee ever took further action, no hearing or markup was scheduled, and the House never voted on the bill before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill drew only three cosponsors, all Democrats, out of 231 House Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans are better off, because they kept the ability to cut provider reimbursement rates and terminate provider contracts during public health emergencies, including COVID-19. Patients and providers who would have gained the contractual protection are left with none.

industries.note: The bill would bar insurers from cutting provider pay or dropping providers during a declared health emergency, removing a cost-control lever they used during COVID-19. Insurers gain when they can shift emergency-period costs onto providers and patients; the bill's death left that lever intact.

Providers' contract terms and reimbursement rates would be locked in during emergencies, protecting their revenue at the moment patient volumes surge. Their gain tracks directly with patients keeping access to in-network care.
